title: Inspecting State
intro: The state file is Terraform's memory of what it built. Reading it safely is the foundation for every state-related fix you'll ever do.

steps.prompt: List every resource Terraform is tracking in state.
steps.fake_output:
aws_instance.web
aws_instance.worker[0]
aws_instance.worker[1]
aws_security_group.web
module.vpc.aws_subnet.private[0]
module.vpc.aws_vpc.main
steps.explanation: Resource addresses: type.name, [index] for count/for_each, and module.name. prefixes for resources inside modules.
steps.why: These exact addresses are what every other state command takes as input — you'll copy-paste from this list constantly.

steps.prompt: Show every attribute Terraform has recorded for the first worker instance.
steps.explanation: Includes computed values like id and private_ip that you never wrote in your config.
steps.why: Quote addresses containing brackets in real shells — [0] can be interpreted as a glob pattern and silently mangled before Terraform even sees it.

steps.prompt: Show the entire state in human-readable form.
steps.explanation: Everything at once — useful for small projects, overwhelming for large ones.
steps.why: 'state show <address>' is the targeted version. For large projects, 'terraform show -json | jq' lets you query specific values across the whole state programmatically.

steps.prompt: Download the raw state file from the remote backend to inspect it locally.
steps.explanation: The raw JSON state, including the 'serial' (incremented on every write) and 'lineage' (identifies this state's history).
steps.why: This is also your manual backup before any risky state surgery. The state file often contains secrets in plain text (database passwords, private keys) — treat any pulled copy as sensitive and delete it when done.
